curve-lab · G3 showcase

G3 showcase · every curve

Cubic Béziers, every join G3 is the lead: six cubic panels, every span four control points. Then the five curves that genuinely need six-point spans. Then every complete curve in one gallery below, grouped by source, so this page gives the overall view. The bell is the cubic exception: eight independent four-point spans, solved for G3; its controls are real, not integer. Inkscape and the glyph pipeline read the four-point spans; a row that cannot be carried by a cubic chain is labelled quintic-required, with the same full fallback on the G3 handover page.

Each panel: the curve; its G3 acceleration dκ/ds with the cuts marked; the construction pipeline (ideal, G3 interpolation, integer cubic spans at ×625); then the handoff table — every control point, the two handle lengths, and the rational slope of each handle. The join error tables are on the G3 notes page.

Why cubic first. A generic cubic cannot carry a G3 join: four control points against the five join conditions. The cases here are the ones where it can — the whole curve is one cubic polynomial, cut at the fifths, so every cut is the same polynomial and all derivatives agree. The quintic G3 span is a degree elevation of each piece; the page shows the collapsed four-point form. The bell is not a cubic, so it cannot collapse: eight independent four-point spans, solved for G3, carry it at a peak error of 7.5e-6. The four-cubic bell is the rejected case; the eight-span chain is the passing one. The circle is G3 everywhere and is explained on the G3 notes page. The G3 catalogue records which other curves admit a quintic interpolation. The gallery below carries every complete curve, with the quintic-required rows labelled; the same set is also on the G3 handover page.

The bell is not a cubic, so it cannot collapse to one. Eight independent four-point spans, solved for G3 at every join, carry it with a worst Δ(dκ/ds) of 6e-13 and a peak error of 7.5e-6. The four-cubic attempt is the rejected case; eight spans are what it takes. The control points are real, not integer.

The finished curve · what can be handed over

The unit is the finished curve, not the span. A curve is G3-complete when every interior join — including the closure seam of a closed form and every mirror seam — matches position, tangent, curvature and curvature-rate, and every break is declared by the source (a cusp, a node, or a singular endpoint), not created by the fit. A smooth handover is a G3-complete curve that is one path with no declared feature, whose deviation is under 5% of its size, and whose spans keep a speed above 10% of their chord. That is the list to give Inkscape or a glyph editor without a smoothness caveat; a curve with a declared cusp or node is still complete, but the feature is what the editor must know about.

The interior-speed gate. A join-only test can pass two spans that each graze a near-cusp in their interior: the ends match, but the span's speed falls toward zero and dκ/ds spikes by many orders of magnitude, flattening the acceleration graph. A span is admitted only when its speed never falls below 10% of its chord. A row that fails is rejected with the measured floor, not drawn flat.

The quintic is the carrier, not the goal. Fixing both endpoints, a G3 join asks for six conditions — tangent direction, curvature and curvature-rate at each end — against eight unknowns in a quintic span; the two left over are the handle lengths used to follow the source. A quartic has no freedom left; a cubic is over-determined. So a quintic span is the least span that can meet G3 at both ends. How many spans there are is a property of the assembly — mirror seams, cusps, nodes and fidelity knots — not of the degree.

Mirror seams are benign, and testable. If a curve crosses a mirror axis orthogonally, reflection preserves curvature (κ is a scalar invariant), so κ is continuous; κ is even about the seam, so dκ/ds is odd and must vanish there. A true mirror of a smooth half is therefore G3 at the seam automatically, and dκ/ds = 0 is the test that the mirror is true. An oblique crossing fails even G1; a mirror tangent — the two arcs meeting with opposite tangents — is a cusp, not a smooth seam, and is declared as one.

The closure seam is not an exemption. Where a closed curve starts is an artifact of the parameterisation, so the seam must pass like any other join. If it fails, re-knot the decomposition or place the seam at a declared node or cusp. The nodal loops (bow, strophoid, bernoulli, nodal, abs-Gerono) declare a node at the seam: complete with that feature, not smooth.

Native degree. A quintic span is a pure degree elevation of a cubic when its fifth divided difference vanishes: P0 − 5P1 + 10P2 − 10P3 + 5P4 − P5 = 0. The fifth-degree freedom then did no work, and the row is badged cubic-native — a simple curve collapsing to a cubic is a selector signal, not an accident. The badge is derived from the control polygon, never asserted. 22 catalogue rows are cubic-native; all five cubic panels on this page are, by construction.

154 G3-complete of 232 candidates · 130 smooth handover · 24 complete with a declared feature. A source corner smoothed inside the 5% tolerance is delivered smooth; the fit flags a singular endpoint only when it had to trim. The gate, and what it refuses

Interior speed. A join-only gate can pass two spans that each graze a near-cusp inside: the ends match, but the span nearly stops and dκ/ds spikes. Every span here is also required to keep a speed above 10% of its chord, and each panel reports its speed floor (59–92% on this page). The interior-speed check is what keeps the acceleration graphs readable.

The join error tables are on the G3 notes page, one per curve, computed from the Bézier derivatives at the join, not from a sampled polyline: position gap, tangent angle, curvature gap and curvature-rate gap. The pass threshold is 1e-9 for the three scalar gaps and 1e-6° for the tangent angle (floating-point noise). The integer cubic's controls are integers at ×625 on the five integer panels; that is a lattice statement about the handles, not a claim that the curve is integer between the cuts. The bell's controls are real; only its span count and G3 data are fixed.

The sections below show the cusp and deviation cases; the main panels remain cubic-only.

Cusp curves · admitted and rejected

A cusp is a declared feature, not a G3 join: the curve is split into smooth arcs between cusps, and G3 applies to the arcs. The admitted family is complete here — astroid, deltoid, nephroid, the epicycloids, the hypocycloid, the cardioid and the cusped heart. Semicubical and pear are rejected cases kept beside them for comparison: their cusp defeats the fit, and the card says so. Cusped hearts: heart · Eisemann lower, heart · Hechinger lower, heart · Kuriscak lower, heart · Kuriscak upper, heart · Mangaldan, heart · Sio lower, heart · Sio upper, heart · Valentine, heart · Wolfram, heart · Wu–Nick lower, heart · cardioid, heart · half-ellipse lower, heart · |x|^(2/3) lower, heart · |x|^(2/3) upper. These are quintic cases, not cubic panels.
